name: Octreotide
subclass: Cyclic disulfide octapeptide with D-Phe, D-Trp and a C-terminal threoninol; SST2-preferring agonist
status_note: Approved since 1988 (Sandostatin) for acromegaly and hormone-secreting neuroendocrine tumours, as a short-acting injection, a monthly intramuscular depot (1998), oral capsules (US, 2020) and a monthly subcutaneous depot (EU and UK, 2025); generic injections have been approved in the US since 2005.
evidence_note: Nearly four decades of clinical use and several randomised trials (for example PROMID in neuroendocrine tumours, phase 3 trials of oral octreotide, and over 20 trials in variceal bleeding), but mostly of modest size and without a large outcome-trial programme.
tagline: Long-acting somatostatin analogue for acromegaly and neuroendocrine tumours
summary: Octreotide is a ring-shaped eight-amino-acid version of the hormone somatostatin, engineered at Sandoz so that it lasts hours instead of minutes. Sold as Sandostatin and in monthly depot and oral forms, it suppresses excess growth hormone in acromegaly and the hormone-driven flushing and diarrhoea of neuroendocrine tumours, and slows the growth of some of these tumours.
overview: Somatostatin was discovered in 1973 at the Salk Institute, when Roger Guillemin's group, searching sheep hypothalami for a growth-hormone-releasing factor, instead found a 14-amino-acid peptide that blocked growth-hormone release. It proved to be a broad brake on hormone secretion in the pituitary, pancreas and gut, but it survives only minutes in the blood and must be given by continuous intravenous infusion, which limited its use as a medicine.

Chemists at Sandoz in Basel set out to shrink the hormone to a stable active core. Starting from a six-residue disulfide ring, Cys-Phe-D-Trp-Lys-Thr-Cys, that carries the receptor-binding Phe-Trp-Lys-Thr turn, they extended both ends: a D-phenylalanine at the front and threoninol, an amino alcohol, at the back. The resulting octapeptide, SMS 201-995, was selected in 1980 and published in 1982; it inhibited growth hormone more potently than somatostatin itself and has a half-life of about 1.7–1.9 hours after injection.

Octreotide (Sandostatin) was first registered in 1988 for acromegaly and hormone-secreting neuroendocrine tumours, in which it controls the flushing and diarrhoea of carcinoid syndrome and the watery diarrhoea of VIPomas. A monthly intramuscular depot followed in 1998, and the PROMID trial (2009) showed that it also slows the growth of metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumours. Radiolabelled versions of octreotide and its close relative octreotate turned somatostatin receptors into targets for tumour imaging (OctreoScan, 1994) and radionuclide therapy (Lutathera, 2018).

Newer formulations aim to replace frequent or deep intramuscular injections: delayed-release oral capsules (Mycapssa, US 2020) that use a medium-chain fatty-acid formulation to carry a small fraction of the peptide across the gut wall, and a once-monthly subcutaneous depot (Oczyesa) authorised in the EU and UK in 2025. Octreotide is also widely used off-label, most notably for bleeding oesophageal varices, and is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines.
mechanism: Octreotide is an agonist of somatostatin receptors, inhibitory G-protein-coupled receptors. It binds SST2 with high affinity and SST5 and SST3 less strongly, with little activity at SST1 and SST4. Receptor activation through Gi/o proteins lowers cAMP and calcium entry and blocks hormone exocytosis, suppressing growth hormone from pituitary adenomas (and so IGF-1), serotonin and peptide hormones from neuroendocrine tumours, and the release of insulin, glucagon, gastrin, VIP and TSH.

It also reduces intestinal fluid secretion, gut motility, gallbladder contraction and splanchnic blood flow, which explains both its anti-diarrhoeal use and its best-known side effect, gallstones. Its antiproliferative effect in neuroendocrine tumours is attributed to SST2/SST5-mediated cell-cycle arrest plus indirect effects on growth factors and tumour blood supply. Cryo-EM structures published in 2022 show the peptide's Phe-D-Trp-Lys-Thr turn inserted deep into the SST2 binding pocket.
origin: Synthetic analogue of somatostatin-14, a cyclic peptide hormone made in the hypothalamus, the pancreatic delta cells and the gut

discovery.by: W. Bauer, J. Pless and colleagues, Sandoz
discovery.note: First synthesised in 1979 and chosen in 1980 as the most stable and potent of a large series of somatostatin analogues; published as SMS 201-995 in Life Sciences in 1982.

first_approval.indication: Severe diarrhoea and flushing of metastatic carcinoid tumours; watery diarrhoea of VIP-secreting tumours

brands.name: Sandostatin
brands.route: Subcutaneous or intravenous injection, 2–4 times daily

brands.name: Sandostatin LAR Depot
brands.use: Acromegaly; carcinoid tumours; VIPomas (UK label also: advanced midgut neuroendocrine tumours)

brands.name: Mycapssa
brands.use: Long-term maintenance in acromegaly after response to octreotide or lanreotide

brands.name: Oczyesa
brands.route: Subcutaneous depot (FluidCrystal) by autoinjector, once monthly
brands.use: Maintenance treatment of acromegaly after response to somatostatin analogues

analogs.name: Somatostatin-14
analogs.note: The native 14-residue hormone; lasts only minutes in blood and is given by intravenous infusion.

analogs.name: Lanreotide
analogs.note: Ipsen's cyclic octapeptide analogue (Somatuline) with a similar SST2/SST5 profile, given as a deep subcutaneous depot.

analogs.name: Pasireotide
analogs.note: Novartis cyclohexapeptide (Signifor) that binds SST1, SST2, SST3 and especially SST5; used in Cushing's disease and acromegaly.

analogs.name: Indium-111 pentetreotide
analogs.note: DTPA-conjugated octreotide for somatostatin-receptor scintigraphy (OctreoScan, FDA 1994).

analogs.name: Lutetium-177 dotatate
analogs.note: DOTA-Tyr3-octreotate, a close octreotide relative, for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (Lutathera, FDA 2018).

analogs.name: Paltusotine
analogs.note: Once-daily oral non-peptide SST2 agonist (Palsonify), approved by FDA for acromegaly in 2025.

modifications.label: D-Phe1: an N-terminal D-phenylalanine added to the ring; it increases potency and protects against aminopeptidases
D-Trp4 (corresponding to Trp8 of somatostatin) stabilises the receptor-binding β-turn Phe-D-Trp-Lys-Thr and resists proteolysis
C-terminal threoninol (Thr-ol): the carboxyl group of the last threonine is reduced to a primary alcohol

sequence.note: Octreotide is numbered 1–8 on its own; residues 3–6 (Phe-D-Trp-Lys-Thr) mimic Phe7-Trp8-Lys9-Thr10 of somatostatin-14. The final residue is threoninol, shown with the Thr token and c_term "ol".

half_life: ≈ 1.7–1.9 h after subcutaneous injection (native somatostatin: a few minutes)

pdb.title: Somatostatin receptor 2 in complex with octreotide and Gi3
pdb.note: Active-state SST2 with octreotide in the orthosteric pocket (Robertson et al., 2022)

pdb.title: Octreotide-bound somatostatin receptor 5–Gi complex
pdb.note: The same peptide bound to SST5, its second main receptor

pdb.title: Octreotide oxalate
pdb.note: Crystal structure of the drug substance (three peptide copies, chains A–C) solved from powder diffraction data

structure.notes: Receptor-bound structures show the Phe-D-Trp-Lys-Thr β-turn reaching into the transmembrane pocket of SST2 or SST5; the NMR and powder-diffraction entries show the free peptide.

approved.detail: Lowers growth hormone and IGF-1 when surgery or radiotherapy is inadequate or not possible; the oral capsule and the monthly subcutaneous depot are licensed for maintenance after response to injected somatostatin analogues.

approved.use: Carcinoid syndrome and other functional gastro-entero-pancreatic tumours
approved.detail: Controls the severe diarrhoea and flushing caused by hormone-secreting neuroendocrine tumours.
Treats the profuse watery diarrhoea of vasoactive-intestinal-peptide-secreting tumours.
Tumour-growth control with the monthly depot, based on the PROMID trial.
When secretion is not normalised by surgery or radiotherapy, or surgery is inappropriate.

approved.use: Bleeding gastro-oesophageal varices; complications after pancreatic surgery
approved.detail: Emergency control of variceal bleeding in cirrhosis and prevention of complications after pancreatic surgery are licensed indications of the short-acting injection in the UK.

investigational.use: Acromegaly: monthly subcutaneous depot in the US
investigational.detail: Camurus' CAM2029 (Oclaiz in the US) received a complete response letter on 10 June 2026 over observations at a third-party manufacturer; FDA accepted a resubmission with a target action date of 18 December 2026.

off_label.detail: Given as an intravenous infusion alongside endoscopic treatment in cirrhosis because it lowers portal and splanchnic blood flow.
off_label.evidence: A 2008 Cochrane review of 21 trials (2,588 patients) found fewer transfusions and fewer failures of initial haemostasis but no significant reduction in mortality.

off_label.detail: Used in toxicology to suppress insulin release and prevent recurrent hypoglycaemia after sulfonylurea poisoning.
off_label.evidence: Supported by case series and small studies rather than large trials.

off_label.detail: Used in infants whose hypoglycaemia does not respond to diazoxide.
off_label.evidence: Observational evidence only; safety in neonates, including gut complications, has been questioned.

off_label.use: Refractory secretory diarrhoea and chyle leaks
off_label.detail: Used for chemotherapy-induced or other refractory diarrhoea, high-output stomas, dumping syndrome and chylothorax.
off_label.evidence: Mostly case series and small trials; practice varies.

history.title: Somatostatin discovered
history.detail: Paul Brazeau, Roger Guillemin and colleagues at the Salk Institute described a hypothalamic peptide that inhibits growth-hormone secretion and named it somatostatin.

history.title: Sandoz selects SMS 201-995
history.detail: Building on the hexapeptide core Cys-Phe-D-Trp-Lys-Thr-Cys, Sandoz chemists identified D-Phe-Cys-Phe-D-Trp-Lys-Thr-Cys-Thr-ol as their most stable and potent analogue and took it into clinical studies.

history.title: Octreotide published
history.detail: Bauer, Pless and colleagues described SMS 201-995 in Life Sciences as a very potent and selective octapeptide analogue of somatostatin with prolonged action.

history.title: First results in acromegaly
history.detail: A single 50 µg injection lowered growth hormone for about nine hours in six of seven people with acromegaly (Lancet).

history.title: Relief of carcinoid syndrome
history.detail: Kvols, Moertel and colleagues reported in NEJM that flushing and diarrhoea were promptly relieved in 22 of 25 patients with metastatic carcinoid tumours given SMS 201-995 three times daily.

history.title: FDA approves Sandostatin
history.detail: First approved in the US for the diarrhoea and flushing of carcinoid tumours and the watery diarrhoea of VIPomas; registrations for acromegaly followed.

history.title: Radiolabelled octreotide for tumour imaging
history.detail: FDA approved OctreoScan (indium-111 pentetreotide), a chelator-linked octreotide used to locate somatostatin-receptor-positive tumours by scintigraphy.

history.title: Monthly depot approved
history.detail: Sandostatin LAR Depot, octreotide in biodegradable polymer microspheres, allowed one intramuscular injection every four weeks.

history.title: First US generics
history.detail: FDA approved the first generic octreotide acetate injections.

history.title: PROMID shows tumour control
history.detail: Octreotide LAR lengthened median time to tumour progression in metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumours to 14.3 months versus 6 months with placebo.

history.title: Radionuclide therapy with an octreotide relative
history.detail: FDA approved Lutathera (lutetium-177 dotatate), built on the closely related peptide octreotate, for somatostatin-receptor-positive gastro-entero-pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.

history.title: First oral somatostatin analogue
history.detail: FDA approved Mycapssa delayed-release capsules for long-term maintenance treatment of acromegaly in people who had responded to injected octreotide or lanreotide.

history.title: Receptor structures solved
history.detail: Cryo-EM structures of somatostatin receptor 2 bound to octreotide revealed how the peptide's β-turn engages the receptor.

history.title: Oral octreotide authorised in the EU
history.detail: Mycapssa received an EU marketing authorisation for acromegaly; it was withdrawn at the holder's request for commercial reasons in February 2025.

history.title: Monthly subcutaneous depot in Europe
history.detail: The EU authorised Camurus' Oczyesa, a once-monthly self-injected octreotide depot for acromegaly; the UK MHRA followed on 28 August 2025.

history.title: Oral non-peptide rival approved
history.detail: FDA approved paltusotine (Palsonify), a once-daily oral non-peptide SST2 agonist, for adults with acromegaly.

history.title: US complete response letter for CAM2029
history.detail: FDA declined to approve the monthly subcutaneous depot pending resolution of manufacturing-inspection findings; a resubmission was accepted in July 2026 with a target date of 18 December 2026.

regulatory.detail: Sandostatin (1988), Sandostatin LAR Depot (1998) and Mycapssa capsules (2020); generic injections since 2005. The CAM2029 subcutaneous depot is under FDA review (target date 18 December 2026).
Sandostatin and Sandostatin LAR are authorised nationally; Oczyesa centrally authorised in June 2025. Mycapssa was authorised in 2022 but withdrawn in 2025 for commercial reasons.
Sandostatin injection authorised since 1989, Sandostatin LAR and generics; Oczyesa approved by the MHRA in August 2025.

pk.half_life: Apparent half-life 1.7–1.9 h after subcutaneous injection
pk.tmax: About 0.4 h after subcutaneous injection; 1.7–2.5 h after an oral capsule; the LAR depot gives a small early peak, then a plateau from about 2–3 weeks after injection
pk.bioavailability: Rapid and essentially complete absorption after subcutaneous injection; a 20 mg oral capsule gives about the same exposure (AUC) as 0.1 mg injected subcutaneously
pk.metabolism: Resistant to peptidases because of its D-amino acids, disulfide ring and threoninol end; cleared by the liver and kidneys
pk.excretion: About 32% of a dose is excreted unchanged in urine

dosing.regimen: Acromegaly: 50 µg subcutaneously three times daily at first, usually 100–500 µg three times daily for maintenance. Carcinoid tumours: 100–600 µg daily in 2–4 divided doses for the first 2 weeks. VIPomas: 200–300 µg daily in 2–4 divided doses at first.
20 mg by intragluteal injection every 4 weeks (after a trial of the short-acting injection), then adjusted according to GH/IGF-1 levels or symptoms.
20 mg twice daily on an empty stomach (at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal), increased in 20 mg steps to a maximum of 80 mg daily.

dosing_note: Labelled regimens summarised for reference only; follow the prescribing information and a clinician's advice.

serious: Gallstones and their complications (cholecystitis, cholangitis, pancreatitis)
Vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
warnings: No boxed warning; labels advise monitoring of the gallbladder, blood glucose, thyroid function and heart rhythm
safety.notes: Because octreotide suppresses insulin and glucagon as well as growth hormone, doses of insulin and other glucose-lowering drugs may need adjusting; labels also flag interactions with ciclosporin (lower blood levels), beta-blockers and bromocriptine. Injection-site pain is common with the monthly depot, and the short-acting injection is stopped at least 24 hours before each lutetium-177 dotatate dose.

facts: Octreotide keeps the Phe-Trp-Lys-Thr turn that somatostatin uses to bind its receptors, but with the tryptophan in its mirror-image D-form to resist enzymes.
Native somatostatin lasts only minutes in the blood; octreotide's half-life is about 1.7–1.9 hours, and depot forms allow one injection a month.
It ends in threoninol, an amino alcohol, instead of a normal carboxylic-acid terminus.
Radiolabelled octreotide relatives are used both to find (OctreoScan, 1994) and to treat (Lutathera, 2018) neuroendocrine tumours.
Octreotide is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (complementary list).
